newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Chad switches ties to Taipei from China.
newsitem.headline: Chad switches ties to Taipei from China.

text.p: Taiwan said on Tuesday it had re-established diplomatic ties with the Central African state of Chad, scoring a victory in a four decade diplomatic tug-of-war with arch-rival China.

"The Republic of China government, based on mutual respect and co-operation...has resumed diplomatic relations with the Republic of Chad, effective on August 12," the foreign ministry said in an announcement.
The sides have agreed to set up embassies as soon as possible, the ministry said.
The African nation had maintained diplomatic ties with Beijing before switching recognition to Taipei.

The announcement brings to 31 the number of countries that maintain official relations with Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government, although that number will fall to 30 at the end of this year when South Africa switches ties to communist China.

"We are glad to discover that more and more countries can accept the fact of the existence of the Republic of China," Taiwan's Foreign Minister John Chang said at a joint news conference with his Chadian counterpart, Mahamat Saleh Annadif.

"The decision came after years of discussion and careful consideration. Chadian people believe any country in the world has the right to choose its own path, its own fate," Chad Foreign Minister Annadif said.
He said his country believes that Taiwan, like China, has the right to join any international organisations, and that Taipei and Beijing can co-exist.
He declined to comment on possible reaction from China, a bitter rival of Taiwan since the two split after a civil war in 1949.
Annadif said his country wanted to "maintain diplomatic relations" with Taipei and Beijing.
Chang said it was Chad's right to choose which countries to establish diplomatic ties with, and it was not Taiwan's position to obstruct this.
In Beijing, when asked about the switch in ties, a surprised-sounding Chad diplomat declined to comment, saying he had heard nothing of the change in recognition.

The move is certain to anger Beijing, which has viewed Taipei as a renegade province subject to eventual unification with the mainland and has warned other countries against forging ties with the island.
Taiwan established formal ties with West Africa's small twin-island nation of Sao Tome and Principe in May.
Chad, a landlocked and arid state in Central Africa, is one the world's poorest countries. It has population of about seven million people.
Nationalist Taiwan and China have competed aggressively, especially in Africa, for diplomatic recognition, often accusing each other of using large sums of cash and aid to woo potential partners.
Chang said Taiwan has agreed to offer medical, mechanical and agricultural assistance to Chad, a sprawling former French colony on the fringes of the Sahara desert.
But he declined to say whether Taiwan has agreed to give Chad any financial or economic assistance.
"That depends on what economic assistance Chad would recommend (later)," Chang said.
